body: Start with the question every layer asks first and this subject cannot answer: what taxon is it? A xenobot is built from Xenopus laevis cells, so the CELLS have a taxon. The thing does not. Find out what each layer does when handed the taxon of its parts.

body: the blueprint comes back for Xenopus laevis: 13 organ systems, 67 organs, 214 tissues, 259 cell types. Every term is correct and the whole thing is about the wrong subject. That is a frog. A xenobot has no organ systems, no heart, no gut and no nervous system; it is a ball of skin and heart cells with cilia on the outside. The anatomy layer can describe the DONOR and has no way to express "an assembly of cells from this donor, in an arrangement the donor never makes".

detail.the_gap: There is no construct layer. The blueprint vocabulary is taxon -> organ system -> organ -> tissue -> cell, and a xenobot is a cell-level assembly with nothing above it. Uberon has no term for it because it is not anatomy, and asking for one would be asking the ontology to describe an object that did not exist when it was written.

why: the blueprint into the studio AS A CONSTRUCT, with what it is and is not stated

detail.caveat: This document describes a CONSTRUCT: an assembly made FROM a taxon, which is not an instance of that taxon. The distinction is the whole point of the field. A xenobot is built from Xenopus laevis cells and is not a frog: it has no organ systems, no gut, no gonads and a working life of days, and the donor's anatomy, life history, ecology and predators are facts about the donor and not about it. base.taxon still carries the DONOR, because the cells really are that taxon and the genome really is unedited, so genotype questions are answerable; everything organismal is not. Any tool that reads a taxon from this document must say which of the two it is answering about, and the ones that cannot tell the difference refuse.

body: The locomotion layer is the first one that does not need to know what kind of thing this is. It needs a length, a speed, a medium and a gait. A xenobot has all four, and the taxon it carries is only used for the flight modes. Ask it about ciliary swimming.

why: does a ciliated millimetre-scale construct move, and does its beat produce its speed?

body: nothing this layer can check contradicts the design. That is NOT a finding that it moves: there is no muscle here, no metabolism, no control and no energy budget, and 1 of the 3 checks are regime indicators that never fail anything. Re is of order 5.0e-1, which the convention in media.json puts inside the creeping regime, though at the very top of it where inertia is beginning to matter. The asymmetry between the power and recovery strokes is exactly what the theorem requires: two paths, not one path retraced. That asymmetry is the reason cilia are shaped the way they are, and it is a property of the GAIT, which no part list contains.

theorem.reading: the stroke is declared non-reciprocal (4 degrees of freedom), so the theorem does not forbid it at any Reynolds number.

why: the control: would the layer catch a reciprocal design at this size?

body: the same construct with a single-hinge flap instead of cilia: impossible. IMPOSSIBLE, by a theorem and not by a simulation: the stroke is time-reversible (declared reciprocal) and Re <= 0.498 everywhere in the stated ranges. In the Stokes limit the displacement over a cycle depends on the PATH through configuration space and not on the rate, so a path that retraces itself returns the body exactly where it started. Net displacement per cycle is zero, at any beat frequency. This is the control for the check above -- a layer that returned "fine" for both would not be telling us anything about either.

asked: a 0.5-1 mm ciliated construct swimming at 0.1-0.5 mm/s

body_length_m.source: DESIGN INPUT, swept: 0.5-1 mm across, the order of size a xenobot is described at. Not measured here.

speed_m_s.source: DESIGN INPUT, swept: 0.1-0.5 mm/s. The speed the design is asked for; not measured on any construct here.

gait.description: cilia beating in metachronal waves: the power stroke is extended and nearly straight, the recovery stroke is curled and close to the surface, so the two follow DIFFERENT paths

cycle_hz.source: DESIGN INPUT, swept: ciliary beat frequency asked of the design.

distance_per_cycle_m.source: DESIGN INPUT, swept: net advance per beat.

gait.source: DESIGN INPUT: the propulsion the design proposes, which is the propulsion xenobots are described using

genotype.note: unchanged: the construct is unedited donor cells.

what_it_taught: The locomotion layer is the only one in this run whose subject is actually the construct, because it asks for quantities rather than for an identity. The ciliary design is not contradicted; the same construct with a single-hinge flap is impossible by theorem, which is the control that makes the first answer worth having.

body: The design was asked to DO something: move loose particles into piles. That is not a shape, not a gait and not a scenario in this engine. Ask the functional layer, which is the one that exists to say what a design is for.

why: is the TASK expressible anywhere in this system?

body: the function registry holds four functions, all of them about fish and flight, and nothing about manipulating objects. The closest analogue it can name is flying fishes. A task -- a thing the organism DOES TO THE WORLD, as distinct from a way it moves -- has no representation here at all.

detail.gate: FAIL: the desired phenotype names no function in the registry (glides_over_water, enlarged_paired_pectoral_fins, sustained_powered_flight, high_altitude_o2_handling), so this ledger is about a DIFFERENT function and establishes nothing about the one requested. Not a measurement failure: an out-of-scope request.
detail.function_asked_for: glides over water after leaving it
detail.function_signal: UNMATCHED, not inferred: a desired phenotype WAS supplied ("a millimetre-scale ciliated construct that pushes loose particles into piles as it moves") and it names no function in this registry (glides_over_water, enlarged_paired_pectoral_fins, sustained_powered_flight, high_altitude_o2_handling). The function below ("glides_over_water") came from the design's identity (xenobot-gen0) and is NOT the one requested, so this ledger does not answer the question that was asked.
detail.the_gap: Three dimensions were asked for across these runs and the system has layers for two. Shape: the blueprint. Motion: the locomotion layer, added in this run. Task -- what the thing accomplishes, with what effect on what else -- has nothing. For a xenobot that is the entire point of the object.

why: can it actually move what it was asked to move?

body: The answer changes inside the stated ranges: 0.132x the force needed at the worst corner and 13.236x at the best. Narrow an input and ask again.

detail.model: Stokes drag, F = 6*pi*mu*a*v. Exact for a sphere in the creeping limit.
detail.model_caveat: Drag on an isolated sphere in an unbounded fluid. A particle resting on a surface also has friction and adhesion, which are often LARGER than the drag and are not modelled here; particles in a pile shield one another, which this does not model either; and a non-spherical particle has a different coefficient. Treat the force here as a lower bound on what the task needs.
cannot_say: whether the design can GET to the particle, aim at it, or hold on to it: there is no control model
whether a pile forms: moving particles and accumulating them are different problems, and the second is about where they are released
how long it would take, or whether the organism can pay for it

why: the check said narrow an input and ask again, so narrow it and ask again

body: At every corner of the stated ranges the declared thrust exceeds the drag: 5.00e-10 N against the 3.78e-10 N needed to move 2 particles of radius 0.00001-0.00005 m at 0.0002 m/s through water. Margin 1.324x to 13.236x. The design did not get stronger between these two calls: the CLAIM got narrower, from twenty particles at once to two. That is the loop working as intended -- the check named the corner that failed, and the honest response was to stop claiming that corner.

The functional registry still holds nothing like it -- four fish-and-flight functions -- but the parser reads "sweeps loose particles into a pile" as a manipulation requirement, the routing block sends it to performance_check, and the answer comes from Stokes drag against a declared thrust: The answer changes inside the stated ranges: 0.132x the force needed at the worst corner and 13.236x at the best. Narrow an input and ask again. Shape had a layer, motion got one, and what the organism DOES now has one too.

body: Last, the ecology layer, which should refuse hardest of all. Occurrence records are records of somebody finding the thing somewhere. A xenobot has never been anywhere outside a dish, so there is nothing to find and nothing to find it.

why: ask the occurrence databases about a thing that has no records, and check it refuses

body: asked about "Xenobot" the layer refuses: GBIF could not match "Xenobot" to its backbone taxonomy. Without a key there are no occurrence records to read.

detail.reason: GBIF could not match "Xenobot" to its backbone taxonomy. Without a key there are no occurrence records to read.

why: the donor, which does have records -- and whether they transfer

body: GBIF holds 16,295 occurrence records for Xenopus laevis (Daudin, 1802), concentrated in BE, ZA, US. In the Western Cape, South Africa GBIF holds 20,688 records; the 8 most-recorded non-Aves species are listed. None of the 35 taxa GloBI records as eating Xenopus laevis (Daudin, 1802) appear in this box's top 8 by record count. Read that as a gap in two databases before reading it as an empty niche: the box list is truncated, record-ranked and missing every Aves species. No population parameters were declared, so whether this design could establish against what is there has NOT been evaluated. That question needs numbers no occurrence database contains. Every number here is about Xenopus laevis. A xenobot is 0.5 mm of ciliated donor tissue with no mouth, no gut, no gonads and a working life of days; it shares the genome and nothing else that an ecologist would use. Transferring this community, these predators or this range to the construct would be the error this whole run is about, so the run states the records and does not transfer them.

detail.recorded_range: GBIF holds 16,295 occurrence records for Xenopus laevis (Daudin, 1802), concentrated in BE, ZA, US.
cannot_say: whether the design would be outcompeted: that needs growth rates, carrying capacities and competition coefficients, and none of them is in an occurrence record or an interaction record
how abundant anything is: occurrence counts are records, which is sampling effort as much as biology
whether the design could eat what is there, or be eaten by what is there: the interaction records are for its CLADE, and a design is by construction not its clade
anything about the places nobody has surveyed, which is most places
anything about Aves, which is filtered out of every result here by design and is a central part of most terrestrial communities

asked: could it exist anywhere outside a dish
what_it_taught: Asked about the construct, the occurrence databases have nothing, which is the correct and only possible answer: they record where people found things, and nobody has ever found one. Asked about the donor they answer fully, and none of that answer is about the construct. An ecology layer handed a synthetic object can say where its parts came from and nothing whatever about where it could live.
